metadata.subject: Algebra
metadata.topic: Line through two points: slope (rise over run) and slope-intercept form

annotator.notes: Student flips Δx and Δy in the slope ratio (6−2)/(11−3). Tutor corrects order (change in y over change in x), then guides to m = 2 and y = 2x − 1 with verification hint for (6, 11).

task_context.problem_statement: Find the equation of the line passing through the points (2, 3) and (6, 11).
key_concepts: substituting a point to find b

messages.content: This is the question: Find the equation of the line passing through the points (2, 3) and (6, 11). Please help me solve it.
Start by identifying what information the two points give you. To write the equation of a line, you usually need its slope and one point on the line.
I think I need to find the slope first.
That is the right direction. For two points, the slope compares the change in y to the change in x. Think of it as vertical change divided by horizontal change.
So I should do (6 - 2) divided by (11 - 3), right?

You are using the two differences, but the order is flipped. The numerator should represent the change in y, and the denominator should represent the change in x. Look at the points again and identify which coordinates are y-values.
The y-values are 3 and 11.
Right. So the change in y should come from those two values. The x-values are 2 and 6, so the change in x should come from those. Set up the slope again using change in y over change in x.
It should be (11 - 3) divided by (6 - 2).
That setup matches the meaning of slope. Now simplify that fraction yourself.
The slope is 2.
Now you have the slope. The next step is to use a line form. One common option is y = mx + b. Since you know m, substitute the slope into that form.
So y = 2x + b.
Now use one of the given points to find b. Pick either point and substitute its x and y values into the equation.
I will use (2, 3). So 3 = 2(2) + b.
That substitution is set up properly. Now solve for b without skipping the arithmetic.
Now combine the slope and intercept into the equation of the line.
The equation is y = 2x - 1.
That equation fits the work you showed. As a final check, test the second point, (6, 11), in the equation to make sure it also lies on the line.
